title: Amortized Average Latency via a Single Loop Timer
pattern: Operation latency is reported by timing a whole multi-iteration loop once and dividing the total elapsed time by the iteration count.
why_bad: The division yields a single mean and discards every per-operation sample, so variance, multi-modal behavior and tail stalls (p99, p99.9) become invisible. One 50 ms stall in 10,000 iterations of 5 µs work shows up as a 10 µs "latency" nobody experienced.
detection: An `Instant::now()` (or equivalent) delta taken around a loop of operations and divided by the iteration count, where the result is labelled or reported as latency or per-operation time rather than throughput.
counterexample: Throughput benchmarks that report operations per second and make no latency claim; operations too short to time individually without the timer dominating (a few nanoseconds), where the harness times fixed-size batches and records the per-batch durations in a histogram.
source: Paul E. McKenney, *Is Parallel Programming Hard, And, If So, What Can You Do About It?* (2020), Ch. 11, §11.7.4, p. 312; Brendan Gregg, *Systems Performance* (2013), Ch. 2, §2.6.5, p. 57.
